title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
notes: Included because its headline theoretical claim was later shown to be wrong: Reddi et al. (2018) found an error in the convergence proof and gave counterexamples. That is a claim about a theorem, not an experiment, so it is annotated as not testable -- a good check that the agent does not try to run experiments against mathematics. The empirical convergence comparisons are small and do reduce well.

claims.text: Adam converges faster than SGD with Nesterov momentum when training a logistic regression model on MNIST.
claims.notes: A small, cheap comparison; logistic regression on MNIST runs in seconds on CPU.

claims.text: Adam converges about as fast as AdaGrad on sparse bag-of-words features.
claims.notes: A claim of equivalence rather than superiority; at reduced scale that reads as inconclusive.

claims.text: Adam reaches a lower training cost than SGD with momentum, AdaGrad and RMSProp when training a multilayer neural network on MNIST.
claims.notes: Same setting shrunk: a small MLP on a MNIST subset.

claims.text: Adam shows only marginal improvement over SGD with momentum on convolutional networks.
claims.notes: The paper itself reports the difference as marginal, so a correct reduced-scale run should not resolve it.

claims.text: The average regret of Adam converges, giving an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate for convex objectives.
claims.notes: A theoretical result, not an experiment. Reddi et al. (2018) later found the proof to be flawed. Reduced-scale experiments cannot settle a theorem either way.

claims.text: Bias correction of the moment estimates matters most at the start of training and with small beta2 values.
claims.notes: A direct ablation: the same optimiser with and without bias correction.
